newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG caretaker leader takes over, pledges peace.
newsitem.headline: PNG caretaker leader takes over, pledges peace.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's government appointed a caretaker prime minister on Thursday, replacing Sir Julius Chan who stood aside in the face of civilian and military demands for his resignation.
Chan's replacement, Mining and Petroleum Minister John Giheno, told reporters he would restore peace to the capital, but said mutinous soldiers who joined the protests should be charged.
"In regard to the soldiers, the mutiny...you break a law, you expect the consequences," Giheno told reporters.

Chan on Wednesday defused this impoverished South Pacific nation's 10-day political crisis by standing aside pending the outcome of an inquiry into a $36 million contract with mercenaries to quell an island rebellion.
Finance Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape also stood aside.
Giheno said he would take on the defence portfolio and commerce Minister Nakikus Konga will take on finance.
The cabinet of Chan's coalition government appointed Forests Minister Andrew Baing as Giheno's deputy.
Giheno said he would relinquish the prime ministership to Chan again if the inquiry cleared the embattled leader.
Asked what would happen if Chan was cleared, Giheno said: "He comes back."
Regular elections are due in June for this rugged nation of almost 4.5 million people.
After a day of celebrations on Wednesday -- soldiers and protesters still had to respect an anti-crime curfew -- Port Moresby returned to normality on Thursday.
Buses were running and shops, businesses and banks were open. Outside parliament house, street cleaners picked up the debris of the protests that finally toppled Chan.

The crisis began almost two weeks ago when military commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan's resignation over the contract with British-based Sandline International to use African mercenaries to crush a secessionist rebellion on copper-rich Bougainville island.

Chan promptly sacked Singirok, but street demonstrations broke out, joined by soldiers who blockaded parliament on Tuesday, trapping almost 100 politicians after a parliamentary motion calling on him to quit was defeated.
Chan's mercenaries had been under order to recapture the vast and abandoned Panguna copper mine, but were forced out of PNG before they could launch an assault.
Market analysts said the return to order might facilitate a longer-term solution to the nine-year secessionist rebellion.
